utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is Case Number IT-95-14/2-A, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Mr. Norman Farrell for the Prosecution, with Wolfgang Sakulin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is Mr. Guarglia not with you today?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It seems that events have overtaken Mr. Guarglia's attendance and he won't be with me today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farrell. For General Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. My name is Mitko Naumovski, attorney from Zagreb, and I speak on behalf of Mr. Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Bozidar Kovacic and I am here for Mr. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Naumovski, I should tell you that I signed the order this morning in relation to time that you sought in relation to your book of authorities. Now, first of all, anything the Prosecution wishes to raise particularly?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a few matters. I don't know if -- they don't relate directly to the issues of detention or any of those issues. They relate to the filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What I should say is we are hoping that we can give you a hearing date, the parties a hearing date, in the last quarter of this year. So we would have to know somehow how your disclosure problems are going.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you for the information about the possible hearing date. Regarding the disclosure issues we, at the last status report, had indicated that all the material with respect to the ABiH archives had been disclosed and all the Rule 68 material that we had known about at the time. That needs to be corrected. On May 30th, we disclosed to the Defence 18, approximately 20 logbooks or -- it's hard to describe them. They are similar to war diaries or logbooks kept by certain units, brigades, and others, from the ABiH collection. As you know, under the order by the preappeal judge, yourself, the Prosecution was to have disclosed a number of documents which, as set out in the order, had, I think, eight or nine categories. Those documents were disclosed, with the exception of these approximately 20 logbooks or war diaries, as they did not come up when we searched them. They are all handwritten and therefore were not electronically searchable. Therefore, we went through the whole 50.000 documents to check for all those which were not covered by an electronic search. It's extremely onerous and also, to be frank, frustrating to try and find these. I apologise to that. They are disclosed on CD form to the Defence at that time on May 30th, and one part of one was given in hard copy as we didn't have it, we couldn't scan it in electronically. Secondly, with respect to disclosure, there was also disclosed on May 30th a logbook, an HVO logbook. As a result of our search for handwritten notebooks or logbooks or war diaries from the ABiH collection, we went back and searched all the Croatian archive collection in our possession for anything that was handwritten that may not have been retrieved when we did our extensive electronic searches. As a result, we found one operational zone of central Bosnia logbook during the relevant time period, in 1993, which is approximately 400 pages. The Prosecution doesn't contend that the total 400 pages of the logbook is necessary or at all relevant, but we simply gave it to the Defence, as opposed to going through it and trying to pull out those parts that may be relevant under Rule 68. They can look at the complete HVO central Bosnia operative zone logbook for February to August 1993. The last issue, Your Honour, with respect to disclosure, and we've informed the Defence in writing a few days ago, more than a few days ago. But in any event, the last thing, the third thing, is that we are also looking through the rest of our Croatian archive collection for any other HVO logbooks which are handwritten and which would not have, possibly would not have, been found through an electronic search. Without explaining the whole details to you, as you're aware from the materials that have been filed so far in this case, the searches are conducted electronically by search words, and it is of all material that has been put into an electronic data collection. And in this case, some of the material which is handwritten does not actually make it into the data collection, the electronic collection, because it's handwritten and cannot be searched electronically. We have found at the moment between five and eight further handwritten notebooks from the HVO, and we are looking to see the time frame and the relevance. They are now being retrieved. I've informed both counsel for Mr. Kordic and Mr. Cerkez of those issues and they have received two of the three categories of reference. I have other comments to make on other issues, but that's what I have to say on the disclose issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But I recall the last status report referred to some area of disagreement between the parties about some Rule 68 material, or am I confusing it with one of the other cases that we're hearing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I know that that's in Krstic, yes sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You understand it's sometimes difficulty to keep all these separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Same problem, Your Honour. If I could go then to the other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The second issue I wanted to bring to your attention was that the Prosecution has reviewed, in a cursory fashion, the Kordic reply, which was filed on the 12th of June. It's their reply to the Prosecution's supplementary respondent's brief. Just want to put the Court and counsel for Mr. Kordic on notice that the Prosecution, as a result of its initial review, at least initially, is of the view that the material filed in the reply is not directly responsive to the court order of May 22nd and is outside the scope of what was requested in the order, and is not related to the Prosecution's filing either. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are there some new grounds of appeal there?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It Depends on how you read your order, but your order was they were to determine whether or not there was a miscarriage of justice as a result of the denial of the motion for acquittal. The reply brief and the Prosecution's submission actually sets out all the arguments why a motion for acquittal should have been given and what the proper tests should be under Rule 98 bis. In my respectful submission, that was not what was argued by the Prosecution, nor is it what was required by the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you mean that they have gone beyond what was in the original appellants' brief on this question of motion for acquittal?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Some new test that's stated? I haven't read it frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It says that the Trial Chamber should apply the test at the 98 bis stage beyond a reasonable doubt and it argues why the Trial Chamber was wrong in the application of the standard to be applied under 98 bis, and then argues why he should have been acquitted on the motion for acquittal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you saying that their argument is the Trial Chamber itself should have been satisfied of the guilt beyond reasonable doubt, on the evidence up to that stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Up to that stage. It's the same test that was applied in Jelisic, as you recall, at the 98 bis stage they said, at the stage where you bring a motion for acquittal, the Trial Chamber must decide that on the basis of all the evidence before them, applying a test beyond a reasonable doubt, that they could convict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, that's what almost every other Trial Chamber has done. Is there evidence upon which a reasonable Trial Chamber could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt? That is the test that has been applied by all except Jelisic, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. I'm sorry, the other way around, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So, are they seeking to depart from that? There was an argument before the Trial Chamber here that they should have been satisfied themselves beyond reasonable doubt that he was guilty; in other words, they accepted the evidence at the stage when the motion for acquittal was refused. And the Trial Chamber rejected that argument, and I think every other Trial Chamber has rejected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I may be wrong in this, and I have only read it quickly this morning, and I wanted to raise it. So I'll take a look at it again. But, yes, I accept your reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If they are seeking to resurrect that argument that was rejected by the Trial Chamber, you won't have very much difficulty in responding to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No. We may not have to file anything in response. The issue relates also, or more so, to whether or not they have addressed what was in the order of May 22nd, which is how the failure of the decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If they have presented nothing, then they will probably find a rather dismal result for them on the issue in the appeal. They have been given clear instructions on what to do. If they haven't done it, then that's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Then we will limit our determination to whether they have addressed the scope of the issue assigned to them in the 22nd May. If it's outside of that, then we won't seek to file anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If there is something -- If there is yet another attempt to put on a new ground of appeal, then you can come along and seek leave to respond to it. I hope there isn't. But if there is, you must have the right to reply to it. But that particular issue, I would have thought would not get anybody very far in this day and age.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. The third issue which is really simply just to -- it's more of a notice to the Defence counsel. I was going to attempt to speak to them this morning, before the hearing, but I came a little late. I just wanted to bring to their attention to one of their grounds of appeal relates specifically to whether Article 5 requires a state policy or state plan, and they were permitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It has just been disposed of in Kunarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct. Paragraph 98 of that judgement deals with that issue. I just wanted to bring it to their attention. It may be something they wish to address. Of course, they can reargue it, if they wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No they can't. They would have to demonstrate some reason why they would want to reargue something that has been determined so recently. That's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Those were the three issues, the disclosure, the scope, the reply --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, because it's quite difficult to follow this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid we're all at fault, Mr. Farrell. Are you able to give us any idea at all when you think that this business of the documents will be completed, because we then will give a direction as to when the Rule 115 applications must be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: At this point, I'm sorry, but I will undertake to file something within a week or so, indicating to you how long I think it will take once we've had a chance to have a look at the logbooks and see how big they are and what reviews are required, if that's satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I think you've been calling them status reports, which is fair enough. If you can put another one on when you are in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, any matters you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no issues to raise. As for what my learned friend has said, I do not wish to respond to it. The Defence has made attempts to fulfill your instructions of the 22nd of May. So I will not enter into an argument on this question now. I can only confirm, Your Honour, that what my learned friend, Mr. Farrell has said is true. The OTP has supplied us with some documents, and we received the last CD-ROM I believe about two weeks ago. As for documents, we are now waiting for Registry to deliver to us the documents from the Blaskic appeal case, according to your order, and we hope to receive this in due course so that we can define our position in relation to the motion under Rule 115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There are so many of Blaskic motions. Your application for access has been dealt with finally, has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, we have already received permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I thought there had been an order, but I was wondering whether one of those which still remains to be dealt with also deals with this case. Well, then, have you got any estimate of when you think that this inspection of documents will be completed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour. We have already said we don't know how much there is. We don't know how many documents we will receive from the Blaskic case and how much the OTP will deliver. We have all worked very hard on the motions we submitted on the 12th of this month so that I have not had time look at the latest CD-ROM received from the Prosecution which contains hundreds and hundreds, maybe a thousand pages of documents. So it is impossible at this point to estimate how much time I will still need. But as soon as the OTP delivers the final list of documents under Rule 68, we will know. Then we will know where we stand. I apologise. I still feel that Your Honour could give us some six weeks after discovery from the Blaskic case is completed so that we can then draw up our motion under Article 115 -- under Rule 115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My recollection was we said we would give you 60 days, but we would be prepared to hear what you want to say about it. I think we can't make any final decision as to how long until we know what you're facing, but your description of already being a thousand pages from one source rather dismays me. You did understand, however, we are anxious for this appeal to be heard this year. And on our present timetable, we will have time in the last quarter of the year. So that's when we are hoping to get the appeal on. Rule 115 in itself takes a little time. It's a very daunting prospect in the present case when I hear the number of documents that you may be seeking to tender. But as long as you keep that in mind so that when the documents are presented to you, you're working on them, and we can finally get down to fixing some dates. Is there anything else you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only perhaps two underlying -- one thing: The Defence really wishes to have this case completed as soon as possible. It has been going on for a long time. But sometimes we are faced with insurmountable difficulties. I think that Your Honour is aware of the fact that after we submitted our appeal in August of last year, and then we received about 41.000 pages of new documents from the Prosecution alone. Perhaps even more, because no one has counted. And then there are other documents we have received, and finally the documents we have asked for from the Blaskic case. So this is an enormous volume of documents to look through, but I hope we will be able to do this as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. So do I. But thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, do you want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I have nothing to add to this. I agree with what Mr. Naumovski has said. We have been looking at all the disclosed documents, disclosed from two sources: On the one hand, from the OTP under Article 68; on the other hand, from the Registry on the basis of several orders issued by this Trial Chamber, and also from other cases. When earlier you asked us to tell you when we might be ready to submit our brief under Rule 115, we said that 60 days was quite realistic. I can say that, as far as my Defence is concerned, I can file within the next four or five weeks, as far as the documents I have already looked through are concerned. However, as soon as we get some new documents, then new things crop up, and things change. And you know, of course, what this process looks like. So in any case, I wish to confirm what my colleague has said. It is not in the interests of the Defence to slow down these proceedings. I'm convinced that nothing we have done from the beginning of the appeal has been done, either on purpose or by accident, to cause a delay. On the other hand, we understand and respect the circumstances that are what they are. No one can influence these. It's true that the OTP has acquired new documents, that the archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which are very important to us, are enormous. It is true that some of these documents are written by hand and cannot be searched through electronically. It is also true that sometimes the Registry needs a lot of time to process the materials falling under the order issued by Your Honour for the provision of these materials. Unfortunately, we still do not have the confidential material from the Blaskic appeal case. You issued an order under which we are to be provided with these documents, but there are still some technical problems in relation to Rule 70(C), and we will receive these materials sooner or later. For us, it is the time we receive the documents that is relevant, rather than the time when Your Honours' order was issued. As soon as we receive them, we will work with all possible speed. And I do not believe that these materials will be so voluminous that we will not be able to complete our briefs under Rule 115 within 60 days. We will be very glad to explain anything further Your Honour may wish to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In relation to applications for Rule 115, admission of documents, the Appeals Chamber can only consider the documents all at the one time. It's no good, as it was attempted, for example, in Kupreskic, to deal with them piecemeal. Because what may have little worth when you see it amongst one bundle of documents may become very much more important when you see another bundle of documents. So the final decision under Rule 115 can only be made after all the documents are in. That doesn't prevent you from starting to prepare your applications, as you would understand. But obviously, we cannot make any final decision until all of the Rule 115 documents have been tendered. Now, my statement that we are hoping to list this appeal in the last quarter of this year was intended only to explain to you that is the best time from our point of view. But we are certainly not going to foreshorten any time you have to prepare documents or prepare applications in relation to documents, if the sheer magnitude of the documents causes problems. My only concern in saying that we would hope that we can list this towards the end of the year is that that would be the best time for everybody, if it's possible from your point of view. So don't think that I'm trying to suggest that you have been delaying the matter in any way. It's just that would be the best time. If it can't be then, well then it can't be then. We'll have to come back to it later. Now, is there anything further you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wished, if I may, in response to your explanation, to add that I have an opportunity -- I would like to ask the Court to have a single bundle rather than several because I think it is better for us to submit to the Chamber everything that is new in a single package, and we certainly agree with this method because we feel it's useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Anything in reply, Mr. Farrell?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much for attending today. We'll now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: adjourned at 3.25 p.m.
